title: Kraepelin sorts the psychoses

confidence.note: The split appears in the sixth edition of Kraepelin's textbook, published in 1899. That it underlies modern classification is widely accepted; whether his two disease groups are natural entities is increasingly questioned.

summary: A German psychiatrist sorted madness by how it unfolded over years, splitting the psychoses into two great families that still shape diagnosis.
body: In the sixth edition of his psychiatry textbook, published in 1899, Emil Kraepelin divided the major psychoses in two. *Dementia praecox*, a term borrowed from the French psychiatrist Bénédict Morel, gathered catatonia, hebephrenia and chronic delusional states into one illness with, as Kraepelin saw it, a poor prognosis. Manic-depressive insanity absorbed the recurrent and circular mood illnesses, which he judged to carry a better outlook. Kraepelin classified by symptoms, course and outcome rather than by unproven theories about causes, drawing on records of thousands of patients. Today's diagnostic categories are still recognizably Kraepelinian, though critics doubt that his two categories are natural kinds.

links.note: Kraepelin's course-based method needed long-term observation of patients, which institutions made possible.
Born the same year, Freud classified by hidden causes, Kraepelin by visible course.

title: Freud and the talking cure

confidence.note: Both books are firmly dated; the *Interpretation of Dreams* is dated 1899 by some sources and 1900 by others (its Deuticke imprint reads 1900). Freud's influence is not in doubt; whether his theory is science, and how well the founding cases went, has been contested from the start.

people: Sigmund Freud (1856–1939), Viennese neurologist, founder of psychoanalysis
Bertha Pappenheim (1859–1936), Breuer's patient 'Anna O.', later a social worker and feminist leader
summary: A young Viennese woman named the 'talking cure'; Sigmund Freud turned it into psychoanalysis, the most influential and most contested theory of the mind.
body: In 1895 the Viennese physicians Josef Breuer and Sigmund Freud published *Studies on Hysteria*. Its best-known case, "Anna O.," was Bertha Pappenheim, whom Breuer had treated for partial paralysis and hallucinations; describing her traumatic experiences seemed to bring relief, and she named the process the "talking cure." Freud, who had found the effects of hypnosis short-lived, took up Breuer's method and argued that many neuroses grew from forgotten traumatic experiences that could be recalled and discharged.

Breuer balked at Freud's growing emphasis on sex, and Freud went on alone. *The Interpretation of Dreams*, dated 1899 by some sources and 1900 by others (the Deuticke imprint reads 1900), argued that dreams express hidden desires and became the founding text of psychoanalysis, often described as the first major systematic form of psychotherapy.

Its scientific standing was contested from the start. The philosopher Karl Popper argued that a genuine scientific theory must be testable, and critics charged that psychoanalysis could explain any behavior and so ruled nothing out. In 1952 the psychologist Hans Eysenck challenged whether psychotherapy worked at all, pushing the field toward controlled trials.

myth.tradition: Breuer's talking cure freed Anna O. of her hysteria, proving the method.
myth.record: Breuer's treatment was not nearly as successful as he and Freud claimed. Bertha Pappenheim recovered only later, and went on to become an innovative social worker and a leader of the German women's movement.

links.note: The rival way of ordering mental illness: by visible course, not hidden cause.

title: Röntgen sees through skin

confidence.note: The date, the paper and the prints Röntgen mailed out are all documented. Others had produced X-rays without recognizing them, but there is no serious dispute that Röntgen was the first to identify and describe them.

people: Anna Bertha Röntgen, née Ludwig, his wife, whose hand was radiographed
summary: A physicist noticed a screen glowing across a darkened room. Within weeks, the whole world had seen the bones inside a living hand.
body: Late on Friday 8 November 1895, in his laboratory at the University of Würzburg, Wilhelm Conrad Röntgen was passing an electric discharge through a vacuum tube shrouded in black card when a paper screen coated with barium platinocyanide, as far as two meters away, began to glow. Something invisible was escaping the tube and passing through the card. Not knowing what it was, he called it X-rays.

For about six weeks he kept the discovery to himself, testing what the rays could pass through. On 22 December he placed the hand of his wife, Anna Bertha, over a photographic plate; the print shows her bones and a ring, with the flesh a faint shadow. At the end of December his paper "On a New Kind of Rays" appeared in the proceedings of Würzburg's Physical-Medical Society, and on 1 January 1896 he mailed reprints and prints to physicists including Lord Kelvin, Henri Poincaré and Hendrik Lorentz. The Vienna newspaper *Die Presse* broke the story on 5 January.

The news spread fast because almost every physics laboratory had the tubes to repeat the experiment. Within weeks an X-ray located a bullet in a patient's leg in Canada; within a year Glasgow Royal Infirmary had a radiology department imaging kidney stones and a penny lodged in a child's throat. Röntgen never patented the discovery. In 1901 he received the first Nobel Prize in Physics.

The cost came almost as quickly. Thomas Edison reported sore eyes in March 1896, and the *British Medical Journal* described burned hands in April. One study of the radiologists' book of honor estimates that a beginner's risk of eventually dying from the work was up to 10–25 percent in 1896, against 1–2 percent in the years just after.

myth.tradition: Someone else, usually Nikola Tesla, really discovered X-rays before Röntgen.
myth.record: Several researchers produced X-rays unknowingly: Arthur Goodspeed in Philadelphia recorded a shadow image of coins in 1890 without understanding it, and Tesla's early work cannot be checked because much was lost when his laboratory burned in March 1895. Röntgen was the first to identify the rays, investigate them and describe their properties.

links.note: Within months doctors were treating patients with the new rays.

title: Radium and the first radiotherapy

confidence.note: Each early treatment is dated by contemporary reports, but who counts as the first radiotherapist is still argued. Grubbe's long-repeated claim to priority has been judged unconvincing by historians of radiotherapy.

place: Hamburg, southeastern France, Vienna and Paris
people: Emil Grubbe (1875–1960), Chicago practitioner who later claimed priority
summary: Within months of Röntgen's discovery, doctors were aiming the rays at tumors and birthmarks. Who was first is still argued over.
body: Within months of Röntgen's announcement, doctors turned the rays on disease. Before February 1896 a Hamburg doctor named Voigt reported easing the pain of an inoperable throat cancer. In July 1896 Victor Despeignes, a Lyon-trained country doctor, irradiated a stomach tumor and saw it shrink. From November 1896 Leopold Freund in Vienna treated a five-year-old girl's hairy birthmark. The Chicago practitioner Emil Grubbe later claimed to have been first, but historians largely discount him. After the Curies found radium in 1898, sources could be placed directly on or into tumors.

links.note: The first treatments came months after Röntgen's discovery.
The next great weapon against cancer.

title: Aspirin

confidence.note: Hoffmann's synthesis of 10 August 1897 and Bayer's 1899 trademark are documented. Who directed the work is contested: Eichengrün's claim, made decades later, is supported by the historian Walter Sneader (as summarized by Wood) but Bayer continued to credit Hoffmann.

people: Arthur Eichengrün, Bayer chemist who claimed to have directed the work
summary: A country parson tested willow bark on fevers; 134 years later a Bayer chemist made a stable cousin of its active ingredient. Who deserves the credit is still disputed.
body: In 1763 Edward Stone, a clergyman in Chipping Norton, Oxfordshire, wrote to the Royal Society that dried, powdered willow bark cured the "agues" (fevers) of about 50 people. Searching earlier books, he had found only mentions of the tree's name. Chemists later isolated willow's active principle, and from 1874 synthetic salicylic acid was on sale, but it irritated the stomach.

On 10 August 1897 Felix Hoffmann, a chemist at Bayer, described making acetylsalicylic acid in a pure, stable form fit for medicine; others had made the compound before, but not usably. Bayer registered the trademark Aspirin on 6 March 1899. Within a fortnight of the aspirin work Hoffmann also made heroin.

Credit is disputed. Arthur Eichengrün, whom a leading scientific commentary describes as having directed Hoffmann's work, claimed that his contribution had been expunged from the archives in the Nazi period; the historian Walter Sneader supports that view. Bayer continued to credit Hoffmann.

myth.tradition: Felix Hoffmann invented aspirin to ease his father's rheumatism.
myth.record: The father story is described as a legend by the Science History Institute. Some evidence indicates that Arthur Eichengrün, a Jewish Bayer colleague, played a significant role and was left out of the story as told since the 1930s.

links.note: Stone tried willow as a cheap rival to Peruvian bark for agues.
Hoffmann's other acetylation product, heroin, was sold as a cough remedy.

title: Mosquitoes, malaria and yellow fever

confidence.note: The key experiments are documented in letters and publications. The facts are agreed; how credit should be shared between Ross and the Italian team led by Grassi was bitterly disputed at the time.

people: Ronald Ross (1857–1932), Indian Medical Service surgeon
Walter Reed, head of the US Army Yellow Fever Commission
summary: Within four years, doctors proved that mosquitoes carry malaria and yellow fever, and the Reed Commission asked its volunteers to sign consent contracts.
body: In 1877 Patrick Manson showed that the worms that cause lymphatic filariasis pass through mosquitoes. From 1881 the Cuban physician Carlos Finlay tried to show that mosquitoes spread yellow fever; his experiments failed because he left too little time between a mosquito's two bites. In India, Ronald Ross, coached by letter from Manson, dissected thousands of mosquitoes. On 20 August 1897, his "mosquito day," he found malaria parasites growing in the stomach wall of a dapple-winged mosquito fed on a patient. Moved to Calcutta, he traced the full cycle of bird malaria through common grey (culicine) mosquitoes instead.

In 1898 Giovanni Battista Grassi, with Amico Bignami and Giuseppe Bastianelli, proved that Anopheles mosquitoes carry human malaria, infecting a volunteer on 1 November. Ross alone received the 1902 Nobel Prize, and the rivalry between the two camps was intense.

In Cuba in 1900, Walter Reed's commission showed that mosquitoes transmit yellow fever. Its volunteers signed contracts setting out the risks and paying $100, doubled for anyone who fell ill, a document often cited as a prototype of informed consent.

links.note: The older answer to malaria: bark, then quinine.
Reed's signed contracts are often cited as an early landmark in research consent.
A later chapter in the fight against malaria.

title: Something smaller than bacteria

confidence.note: The 1892 and 1898 papers are documented. What each discoverer understood is a matter of interpretation; Beijerinck's 'living fluid' was wrong in detail, and the particulate nature of viruses was settled only in the 1930s.

people: Friedrich Loeffler and Paul Frosch, German bacteriologists
summary: Sap from sick tobacco plants passed through filters that stopped every known germ and still spread disease. Something smaller was at work.
body: In 1892 Dmitry Ivanovsky pushed sap from diseased tobacco plants through a porcelain Chamberland filter, fine enough to hold back bacteria, and found the filtered sap still caused mosaic disease. In 1898 Martinus Beijerinck repeated the experiment in the Netherlands and drew a bolder conclusion: the agent was neither bacterium nor fungus but a *contagium vivum fluidum*, a contagious living fluid, which he called a virus. The same year Friedrich Loeffler and Paul Frosch showed that foot-and-mouth disease of cattle was also filterable and judged its agent particulate, which proved closer to the truth.

links.note: Germ theory had taught doctors to look for microbes a filter could catch.
In 1918 the cause of influenza was still unknown.

title: Patent medicines and the 1906 Food and Drugs Act

confidence.note: The act and its provisions are documented in the statute and in FDA's own histories; its limits were exposed in court within five years.

people: Harvey W. Wiley, chief chemist of the US Department of Agriculture
summary: Microbe Killer and heroin cough syrup were sold with no federal oversight until 1906, when the US began to police what medicine labels said, though not whether medicines worked.
body: Around 1900 anyone could sell a cure in the United States: William Radam's Microbe Killer faced no federal check, and Bayer marketed its new drug heroin, launched in 1898, to suppress coughs. Journalists such as Samuel Hopkins Adams exposed the trade, and on 30 June 1906 President Theodore Roosevelt signed the Food and Drugs Act. It regulated labels, not safety: alcohol, heroin, cocaine and eight other dangerous ingredients had to be declared. In 1911 the Supreme Court ruled that false curative claims fell outside it.

links.note: Heroin came out of the same Bayer acetylation work as aspirin.
Later disasters pushed US law from labels toward proof of safety and efficacy.
